title: The Day the Sun Stood Still
summary: Five Amorite kings led by Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel. Joshua marches all night from Gilgal, the LORD throws the enemy into confusion and sends deadly hail, and at Joshua's prayer the sun and moon stand still until the victory is complete. The five kings are found hiding in a cave at Makkedah and executed, and Joshua sweeps through the cities of the southern hill country and lowlands.
story: The treaty sworn in chapter 9 now costs Israel something. Because Gibeon has gone over to Israel, the kings of the south see a breach in their defenses and move to punish it. Israel honors its oath by marching to Gibeon's rescue, and the result is the decisive battle for the south. The chapter repeats one refrain in several forms: the LORD delivers, the LORD throws into confusion, the LORD fights for Israel. It carries forward the promise of chapter 1 that no one would be able to stand against Joshua, and it sets up chapter 11, where the kings of the north gather for the same kind of war.
historical:
The five cities named in verse 3 are real places in southern Canaan. Jerusalem sat on the ridge between the hill country and the wilderness. Hebron lay about twenty miles south of it, and Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon were in the Shephelah, the low foothills between the hills and the coastal plain. Lachish (Tell ed-Duweir) was one of the great cities of the region. Jerusalem's kings are known from outside the Bible in this general era: the Amarna letters, clay tablets from Egypt dating to the fourteenth century BC, include letters from a ruler of Jerusalem named Abdi-Heba asking Pharaoh for help against his enemies. The name Adoni-zedek, meaning my lord is righteous or lord of righteousness, recalls Melchizedek, king of Salem, in Genesis 14:18.

The battle route follows real geography. The ascent and descent of Beth-horon was the main road from the Aijalon Valley up to the central plateau near Gibeon, and armies fought along it for centuries; the books of Maccabees record a Jewish victory there in the second century BC. The chapter's summary claim that Joshua conquered the whole region in "one campaign" (verse 42) stands alongside later notes in the same book that Jerusalem was not taken (15:63) and that Hebron and Debir had to be captured again (15:13-17). How these fit together is discussed below.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern kings routinely described their wars as the work of their gods, and they told them in stock phrases: the enemy was routed, cities were leveled, none survived. Assyrian and Egyptian royal inscriptions use this kind of language, sometimes for victories that were far from total. Placing a foot on a defeated king's neck was a common gesture of triumph, pictured in Egyptian and Assyrian art, and it lies behind the biblical image of enemies made a footstool (Psalm 110:1).

Hanging the kings' bodies on trees and taking them down at sunset follows the law of Deuteronomy 21:22-23, which forbade leaving a hanged body overnight because it was under God's curse and would defile the land. Joshua did the same with the king of Ai (8:29). The cave sealed with great stones, still visible "to this day," functioned as a memorial like the stone heaps at the Jordan and at Achor. The Book of Jashar, cited in verse 13, seems to have been a collection of poetry about Israel's heroes; it is quoted again in 2 Samuel 1:18 for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, and it has not survived.
literary: The chapter has two halves. Verses 1-27 tell the battle at Gibeon in vivid detail, with a poetic quotation at its center (verses 12-13) and the narrator's comment that "There has been no day like it before or since" (verse 14). The five kings form a frame: they gather in verses 3-5 and are brought out and killed in verses 22-27. Verses 28-39 then switch to a fast, formulaic report of six cities in sequence (Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir), with the defeat of Gezer's king noted in passing (verse 33). Each report repeats the same phrases: captured it, put it to the sword, left no survivors, as he had done to the previous city. The repetition gives the impression of a relentless sweep, and verses 40-43 sum it up. Verse 15, in which Israel returns to Gilgal before the Makkedah episode, is repeated in verse 43; many readers take verse 15 as the close of the quoted poetic account rather than as a step in the sequence, and the Greek Septuagint lacks both verses.

outline.t: Joshua's night march and the LORD's hail
The five kings in the cave at Makkedah
The southern cities taken one by one

doctrines.note: The LORD rules the weather and the heavens: he sends hail and holds sun and moon in place. The heavenly bodies that Canaan worshiped obey Israel's God. The chapter insists that the victory belongs to him, "because the LORD fought for Israel" (verse 14).

Joshua speaks to the LORD in front of Israel, and the narrator marvels that "the LORD listened to the voice of a man." The chapter presents bold prayer offered in the course of obedience as something God answers.

The conquest is presented as God's judgment on the peoples of Canaan (compare Genesis 15:16 and Deuteronomy 9:5), not as Israel's reward for its own goodness. The same law of judgment will later fall on Israel when it copies their ways.

words.note: Charam, to devote to destruction. It describes giving something wholly over to God so that no human could keep or use it, which in war meant killing the population and destroying or dedicating the spoil. The verb recurs through verses 28-40 as the chapter's refrain.

Damam, to be still or silent. Joshua commands the sun to be still. Because the word can also mean to stop or cease, some interpreters have asked whether the sun stopped moving, stopped shining, or both, which is part of the discussion in the hard question below.

Lacham, to fight or make war. The kings "made war" against Gibeon (verse 5), and the chapter's key claim uses the same verb for God: the LORD fought for Israel (verses 14 and 42). Israel's victories are the LORD's warfare.

Sarid, a survivor. The repeated phrase that Joshua left no survivor belongs to the standard vocabulary of ancient conquest reports, and it must be read alongside the book's own notes that many Canaanites remained in the land.

christ: The strongest link is thematic. Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus, puts his feet on the necks of kings and says the LORD will do this to all Israel's enemies. The New Testament takes up Psalm 110:1, where God makes the enemies of his king a footstool, and applies it to the risen Christ, who reigns until every enemy, death included, is put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). The law about hanged bodies obeyed in verses 26-27 is the very law Paul quotes when he says that Christ became a curse for us by hanging on a tree (Galatians 3:13). In Joshua the curse falls on the enemies of God; at the cross the King himself takes it for his enemies.

hard.q: Did the sun really stand still, and how should we read the claims that Joshua left no survivors?
hard.a:
Readers take the sun and moon miracle in several ways. Some understand it as a literal suspension or slowing of the earth's rotation, or a local miracle of light, pointing out that the text calls the day unique. Others note that the words of verses 12-13 are poetry quoted from the Book of Jashar and read them like other biblical poetry, such as the stars fighting against Sisera (Judges 5:20), as vivid language for a day on which heaven itself seemed to fight for Israel. Still others have proposed that Joshua asked for the sun and moon to stop shining, prolonging the darkness of a storm, or have compared the passage with ancient Mesopotamian texts that read the positions of sun and moon as omens. All of these readers agree that the text credits the victory to God.

The repeated statement that Joshua left no survivors also raises questions, both moral and historical. The book itself says that survivors fled to fortified cities (verse 20) and that Hebron, Debir, and Jerusalem still had to be taken later. Many evangelical and other scholars argue that the language follows the conventions of ancient conquest accounts, which used sweeping, hyperbolic formulas; Mesha of Moab, for example, claimed that Israel had perished forever. Others take the statements more literally. On the moral question, many Christians answer that the Bible frames the conquest as a unique act of God's judgment on a specific culture at a specific time (Genesis 15:16), not a pattern for later wars. Others read these chapters as a stage in Israel's understanding of God that must be interpreted in the light of Christ, and a tradition going back to Origen has read the wars spiritually, as a figure of the struggle against sin (see the note on chapter 6). No one of these answers satisfies every reader, and it is fair to say the difficulty remains a real one.

questions: Israel's oath to Gibeon led it straight into a war. What does it look like to keep faith with someone when doing so brings trouble on you?
Joshua prayed a bold prayer in the middle of obedient action. Are your prayers usually cautious? What would bolder prayer look like?
How do you hold together the chapter's picture of God fighting for his people with the rest of Scripture's picture of God's mercy to the nations?
